title: Your Daily Walk Alone Won't Build Fitness: Intensity, Variety, Strength Training Matter
excerpt: Fitness expert Sumit Dubey says most walkers stall because comfortable-pace strolls never push the heart and lungs — faster intervals, varied routes, and strength work close the gap.
body:
• Walking daily is good for you, but a comfortable-pace stroll barely moves cardiovascular fitness — intensity, not just duration, is the key factor.
  • Repeating the exact same walk every day lets the body adapt; varying pace, distance, and incline with bursts of faster walking re-triggers progress.
  • After age 30, muscle mass declines unless trained; the WHO recommends muscle-strengthening activities for major muscle groups on two or more days per week for adults.
  • Adult guidelines: at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week — like brisk walking — plus strength work, according to the WHO and CDC.

Your walk is a habit, not a training plan

Plenty of people log a daily walk and wonder why their fitness has stalled. A short stroll down the road improves circulation, relaxes the mind, and beats sitting still — but achieving better cardiovascular fitness frequently demands more than a comfortable shuffle around the block. That is the case Sumit Dubey, fitness expert and founder of Sumit Dubey Fitness, made in a recent Hindustan Times interview, and it lines up squarely with what global health guidelines say.

"Intensity is the important factor," Dubey said. "You're unlikely to work your heart and lungs hard enough at a comfortable pace." The research he cites points to a faster pace — fast enough to talk but not sing — doing more for calorie burn and oxygen consumption than an easy stroll. The same distance walked faster is a different workout.

Boredom is the body's adaptation signal

Dubey's second point is about repetition. Walking the identical route at the identical pace and timing every day teaches the body to get efficient at exactly that task — and progress slows. The fix is variety: change the pace, length, or incline, or mix intervals of fast and slow walking into the same outing. The heart, he said, benefits from the change. In practical terms, that means turning a 30-minute walk into alternating two-minute brisk bursts and two-minute easy segments, or adding a hillier route twice a week.

The strength gap after 30

The biggest blind spot, Dubey argued, is resistance training. "Many do not appreciate how walking alone is insufficient without additional resistance work," he explained, stressing that fitness is not one-size-fits-all and depends on the link between heart health, strength, stability, flexibility, and range of motion. After 30, muscle mass declines slowly unless it is worked against resistance. That steady stroll will not stop that shift.

Here the guidance is unambiguous. The World Health Organization recommends adults do at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week — or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or an equivalent mix — and explicitly adds muscle-strengthening activities involving the major muscle groups on two or more days a week. The CDC gives the same dual prescription: brisk walking 30 minutes a day, five days a week, plus strength work on two or more days. Lifting two or three times a week adds what walking misses: higher caloric expenditure, better metabolic function, and refined body control.

"Intensity is the important factor. You're unlikely to work your heart and lungs hard enough at a comfortable pace."

— Sumit Dubey, Fitness Expert and Founder, Sumit Dubey Fitness

Small form fixes, bigger payoff

Dubey also points at posture. Shuffling forward while staring at a phone slows everything down. Lifting the gaze, gently tightening the stomach, and letting the arms move freely makes every step work harder. Walked with intention, the same 30 minutes delivers noticeably more effort through the body — no extra time required.

The diaspora angle: from walking culture to full fitness

Walking is deeply embedded in Indian life and the diaspora — the evening family walk is a cherished routine. The useful upgrade is not abandoning it but layering onto it: a few weekly faster-walk intervals on a weekend morning trail, two short resistance sessions with bands or dumbbells at home, and desk-bound professionals swapping one sedentary evening for a strength day. For NRIs whose families mix evening walks with cricket or badminton on weekends, adding structured resistance work closes the exact gap Dubey identifies.

What to change this week

Keep the daily walk — it remains a solid foundation. Add intensity twice a week (a faster segment where conversation stays possible but singing would not), vary the route or incline, and schedule two 20-minute strength sessions for the legs, hips, back, and core. Small increments beat grand restarts, as Dubey put it: keep pushing forward little by little. This article is informational and not a substitute for professional medical advice — consult your doctor before starting a new exercise routine, especially if you have a heart condition or chronic illness.
